questions.stem: Which statement is the principle of conservation of energy?

options.text: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores
options.explanation: This is the stated principle.

options.text: energy always decreases as it is used
options.explanation: Using energy transfers it; the total is constant.

options.text: energy is created usefully and destroyed wastefully
options.explanation: Neither creation nor destruction happens.

options.text: energy runs out when a machine stops
options.explanation: The energy has transferred to other stores, not ended.

questions.stem: A closed system contains two objects that interact. If object A gains 30 J, what happens to object B?

options.text: B gains 30 J as well
options.explanation: That would create energy within the closed system.

options.text: B loses exactly 30 J
options.explanation: One system’s gain must equal the other’s loss inside a closed system.

options.text: B loses more than 30 J because of dissipation
options.explanation: Dissipation redistributes within the accounting; it does not inflate losses.

options.text: B is unaffected
options.explanation: The transfer came from somewhere.

questions.stem: What does dissipated mean?

options.text: converted back into chemical fuel
options.explanation: Nothing reverses like that in these scenarios.

options.text: destroyed so it no longer exists
options.explanation: Dissipated energy still exists.

options.text: spread out to the surroundings, often by heating and radiation
options.explanation: Dissipation is spreading, usually by heating and radiation.

options.text: stored permanently in the thermal store
options.explanation: It is spread through the surroundings, not parked in one store.

questions.stem: Why is dissipated energy often called wasted?

options.text: because it breaks the conservation law
options.explanation: Dissipation is fully compatible with conservation.

options.text: because it always leaves as sound
options.explanation: Heating is the more common dissipation route.

options.text: because it is destroyed
options.explanation: It is not destroyed; conservation forbids that.

options.text: because it has spread to the surroundings where it cannot be used for the intended purpose
options.explanation: Wasted energy is dissipated energy that no longer serves the purpose.

questions.stem: A kettle boils water. Which transfer is the WASTED transfer?

options.text: energy warming the plastic kettle body
options.explanation: The plastic body’s thermal store gain is not useful for boiling water.

options.text: water turning to steam
options.explanation: Boiling the water is exactly what the kettle is for.

options.text: mains supply to the heating element, electrically
options.explanation: That is the intended first link of the chain.

options.text: element to the water, by heating
options.explanation: Heating the water is the purpose of the kettle.

questions.stem: State what happens to the total energy of a closed system.
questions.modelAnswer: The total energy of a closed system remains constant.

questions.stem: State the two dissipation routes named in the principle’s description.
questions.modelAnswer: Heating and radiation — the two dissipation routes named in the principle.

questions.stem: Explain why a bouncing ball never quite returns to its release height, using the conservation law in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer: At each bounce some energy is transferred out of the ball’s kinetic and elastic stores into the thermal stores of the ball and the floor, and some is radiated away as sound. The energy is not destroyed — the total is conserved — but the mechanical energy available for the rebound is reduced, so each bounce reaches a lower height.

questions.stem: A trampoline jumper reaches the top of a bounce with 500 J in her gravitational store; at the top of the next bounce she has 420 J there. State the energy dissipated between the two tops and name one route it took.
questions.modelAnswer: 500 - 420 = 80 J was dissipated between the two tops; one route is heating of the trampoline canvas and the air (with some sound radiated at the canvas).

questions.stem: In the bat-and-ball impact, which transfer is USEFUL?

options.text: ball thermal store to bat thermal store
options.explanation: No useful purpose is served by heating either way.

options.text: bat kinetic store to ball kinetic store
options.explanation: Sending the ball on its way is the purpose of the strike.

options.text: bat kinetic store to ball thermal store
options.explanation: Warming the ball is not the aim.

options.text: bat kinetic store to surroundings by sound
options.explanation: The crack of the bat is dissipated sound.

questions.stem: How is energy transferred from the bat’s kinetic store to the ball’s thermal store?

options.text: by radiation only
options.explanation: Radiation is the sound route, not the impact route.

options.text: by convection
options.explanation: Convection needs a fluid current; the impact is a solid contact.

options.text: mechanically, due to the impact
options.explanation: The impact’s mechanical work deforms and warms the ball.

options.text: electrically
options.explanation: No circuit is involved.

questions.stem: In the kettle, what is the FIRST store to receive the energy from the mains?

options.text: the plastic kettle’s thermal store
options.explanation: The plastic receives wasted energy later.

options.text: the surroundings
options.explanation: Dissipation comes last.

options.text: the water’s thermal store
options.explanation: The element warms first; the water receives energy from the element.

options.text: the heating element’s thermal store
options.explanation: Energy is transferred electrically to the element’s thermal store.

questions.stem: Which kettle transfer is wasted?

options.text: element to plastic kettle body by heating
options.explanation: Warming the plastic serves no purpose.

options.text: water to steam at boiling point
options.explanation: Boiling is the desired outcome.

options.text: element to water by heating
options.explanation: That is the kettle’s job.

options.text: mains to element electrically
options.explanation: The intended input link.

questions.stem: The bat’s kinetic store loses 200 J in the strike. Which set of destinations could conserve energy?

options.text: 200 J destroyed by friction
options.explanation: Friction transfers; it does not destroy.

options.text: 120 J to the ball’s kinetic store, 50 J to thermal stores, 30 J radiated as sound: 200 J total
options.explanation: The shares sum to exactly 200 J, so the books balance.

options.text: 120 J to the ball’s kinetic store and 50 J to thermal stores: 170 J total
options.explanation: 30 J has vanished, which conservation forbids.

options.text: 220 J to the ball’s kinetic store alone
options.explanation: More energy arrives than left the bat.

questions.stem: State the pathway for each link: (a) mains to kettle element, (b) element to water.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) electrical work from the mains supply; (b) heating from the element to the water.

questions.stem: In the bat-and-ball example, state the two stores that receive WASTED energy.
questions.modelAnswer: Thermal stores — of the ball, the bat and the surroundings — receive wasted energy (with some dissipated by heating and radiated as sound).

questions.stem: Explain why the bat, the ball and the air all end up very slightly warmer after the strike.
questions.modelAnswer: The strike cannot transfer all of the bat’s kinetic energy into the ball’s motion: impact deformation transfers energy mechanically into thermal stores, and heating and radiation dissipate more into the surroundings. Since energy is conserved rather than destroyed, those spreads show up as tiny temperature rises everywhere the wasted energy landed.

questions.stem: A kettle element receives 180 kJ from the mains. 150 kJ ends up in the water and steam. Name the account that holds the difference and state its size.
questions.modelAnswer: The missing 30 kJ sits in wasted transfers — the plastic kettle’s thermal store and the dissipated surroundings — because conservation requires the full 180 kJ to be accounted for.

questions.stem: As the jumper falls towards the canvas, which transfer occurs?

options.text: thermal store to kinetic store
options.explanation: The thermal store is where wasted energy ends up, not the source here.

options.text: kinetic store to gravitational store
options.explanation: That is the rising phase.

options.text: gravitational store to kinetic store
options.explanation: Falling empties the gravitational store into the kinetic store.

options.text: elastic store to kinetic store
options.explanation: The canvas is not yet stretched.

questions.stem: At the lowest point of the bounce, which store holds most of the energy?

options.text: the chemical store
options.explanation: Chemical energy is the jumper’s internal fuel, not the bounce account.

options.text: the gravitational store
options.explanation: The jumper is at minimum height there.

options.text: the kinetic store
options.explanation: The jumper is momentarily at rest at the lowest point.

options.text: the elastic store of the stretched canvas
options.explanation: Maximum stretch means maximum elastic energy.

questions.stem: Why do the bounces get lower each time?

options.text: some energy is dissipated by heating and radiated as sound each cycle
options.explanation: The wasted transfers shrink the mechanical account each round trip.

options.text: gravity gets stronger near the canvas
options.explanation: Gravity is essentially constant over the bounce height.

options.text: the canvas loses its elasticity permanently
options.explanation: The canvas rebounds fine; the losses are thermal and sound.

options.text: energy is destroyed at each bounce
options.explanation: Nothing is destroyed; it is dissipated.

questions.stem: Which pathway delivers fresh energy when the jumper jumps higher from the canvas?

options.text: by radiation
options.explanation: Radiation is an output here, not an input.

options.text: mechanically, from the jumper’s muscles pushing on the canvas
options.explanation: Muscles do mechanical work to refill the bounce account.

options.text: by heating from the sun
options.explanation: Sunbathing does not power the bounce.

options.text: electrically
options.explanation: No circuit is involved.

questions.stem: Between two successive tops, the gravitational store holds 500 J then 420 J. The missing 80 J is:

options.text: impossible to know without measuring sound
options.explanation: Conservation pins the total; the split between routes is the only detail.

options.text: destroyed during the bounce
options.explanation: Conservation forbids destruction.

options.text: dissipated to thermal stores and radiated as sound
options.explanation: The difference is exactly the wasted share of the cycle.

options.text: still in the elastic store at the top
options.explanation: At the top the canvas is unstretched.

questions.stem: State the order of stores in one full trampoline cycle, starting from the top of a bounce.
questions.modelAnswer: Gravitational, then kinetic, then elastic, then kinetic, then gravitational again — with thermal and sound taking wasted shares at each exchange.

questions.stem: State the pathway by which the jumper’s muscles add energy at each bounce.
questions.modelAnswer: Mechanically — the muscles do mechanical work pushing against the canvas.

questions.stem: Explain why the jumper’s body and the trampoline canvas are slightly warmer after a session of bouncing.
questions.modelAnswer: Every stretch of the canvas and every impact dissipates some energy by heating into the canvas and the jumper’s body, and some radiates away as sound. The energy is conserved, but the repeated wasted transfers accumulate as small temperature rises in the materials involved.

questions.stem: A jumper’s first top-of-bounce gravitational store holds 600 J and each cycle wastes 12% of the mechanical energy. State the gravitational-store energy at the third top of bounce.
questions.modelAnswer: Cycle 1: 600 × 0.88 = 528 J; cycle 2: 528 × 0.88 = about 465 J at the third top.
